title: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 5.1 Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables
intro: Construct scatterplots, identify explanatory and response variables, and describe form, direction, strength, and unusual features in context.

moments.title: Paired measurements
moments.text: Each point represents two numerical measurements on the same observational unit.

moments.title: Plot ordered pairs
moments.text: Place each observation at its corresponding x and y values.

moments.title: Choose the axes
moments.text: Put the explanatory variable on x and the response variable on y.

moments.title: Age and vocabulary
moments.text: Use age to explain or predict vocabulary size.

moments.title: Association is not causation
moments.text: A scatterplot alone cannot establish a causal effect.

moments.title: Direction
moments.text: Describe whether responses tend to increase or decrease as x increases.

moments.title: Strength
moments.text: Judge how closely points follow the general pattern.

moments.title: Unusual features
moments.text: Look for clusters and points that do not fit the overall association.

cards.name: Two quantitative variables
cards.text: Record both measurements on the same units; avoid losing the pairing.

cards.name: Axes
cards.text: Use the proposed explanatory variable on x and response variable on y, with units and equal-interval scales.

cards.name: Description
cards.text: State form, direction, strength, and unusual features in context.

cards.name: Claims
cards.text: Use tends to rather than claiming every point obeys the pattern. A scatterplot alone does not establish causality.

questions.obj: Construct a scatterplot from paired measurements
questions.q: The video describes toddler age in months and spoken vocabulary size. Two recorded pairs are (20, 95) and (48, 1780). Explain how to place these observations.

work.text: Use age in months horizontally and vocabulary size in words vertically.
Place the 20-month-old at 95 words and the 48-month-old at 1780 words. Do not sort the two lists separately.
Do not connect toddlers with line segments. The two supplied points alone cannot establish the form or strength of the full 14-toddler relationship.

questions.answer: Each point represents one toddler, retaining that toddler's age and vocabulary measurements.

questions.q: Supplementary example: a scatterplot of roof area in square meters versus installation cost has points close to an upward straight pattern, with one unusually high-cost project.

work.text: Larger roofs tend to have higher installation costs.
The main pattern is approximately linear and strong because most points lie close to a straight trend.
One project has unusually high cost relative to others of similar roof area.

questions.answer: There is a strong, positive, approximately linear association between roof area and installation cost, with one unusually high-cost project.

traps.title: Unpaired columns
traps.weak: Sort each variable separately before plotting.
traps.better: Keep each observational unit's measurements together as an ordered pair.

traps.title: Connecting observations
traps.weak: Join every dot to its neighbor.
traps.better: A scatterplot displays separate paired observations; connecting them can imply an unprovided sequence.

traps.title: Cause from direction
traps.weak: A positive association proves that x causes y to rise.
traps.better: A positive association means larger x values tend to accompany larger y values; causality needs design evidence.

traps.title: Incomplete description
traps.better: Name a positive association in context and describe form, strength, and unusual features.

questions.stem: A study uses parcel mass to predict handling time. Which axes are appropriate?
opts: Time on x; mass on y
Mass on x; time on y
why: This reverses the proposed explanatory role.
Mass is explanatory and handling time is the response.
A scatterplot needs paired measurements of two variables.

questions.stem: A plot has points tightly clustered around a downward straight trend. Which description fits?
why: The trend is downward and approximately straight.
The points are tight, so the association is strong.
Tight, downward, straight captures strength, direction, and form.

questions.stem: Which action destroys the information needed for a scatterplot?
opts: Using a common numerical scale on each axis
Keeping each pair in one row
why: The original pairings would be lost.
Each axis needs a sensible equal-interval scale.

questions.stem: Which conclusion can a scatterplot alone support?
opts: The exact cause of every response
A description of the observed association
why: Causal explanations are not determined by a plot.
A plot does not guarantee future responses.
An effect needs the study design and analysis.
The form and direction can be described from the data.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: For five gardens, recorded pairs of daily sunlight in hours and harvested mass in kilograms are (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 6), (5, 7), and (6, 8).
parts: (a) Specify how to construct the scatterplot and identify its observational units.
(b) Describe the observed association in context.
(c) Assess the claim that an extra hour of sunlight must cause a larger harvest.
sample: (a) Each garden is a unit. Plot sunlight on the x-axis and harvested mass on the y-axis with labeled units and numerical scales, preserving the five pairs.
(b) Gardens with more sunlight tend to have greater harvested mass. The five points follow a strong, positive, approximately linear pattern without a clearly isolated point.

(c) The observational pairs alone do not show causation. Other variables such as soil quality could be related to both sunlight exposure and harvest. The observed pattern also does not guarantee every future garden's result.
checklist: Specifies axes, units, and preserved pairs.
Describes form, strength, and unusual features cautiously.
